title: Given a string containing the bracket characters round, square, and curly, determine whether every opening bracket is closed by the matching type in the correct order, using a stack.
shortTitle: Validate Balanced Parentheses Using a Stack
keyPoints: Push each opener onto a stack; on each closer, pop and verify the top is the matching type.
Two failure conditions: empty stack on a closer (unmatched close) and non-empty stack after the scan (unmatched open).
A Map from closer to expected opener keeps matching clean and extensible.
Time is O(n); space is O(n) worst case when all characters are openers.
ArrayDeque is preferred over the legacy synchronized Stack class.
This stack discipline is the foundation of real parsers for XML, HTML, and expression validation.

s1_definition.oneliner: Push every opener, pop and type-match on every closer, and the string is valid only if the stack ends empty.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Balanced Parentheses** – validate that every opening bracket has a matching closer of the same type in the correct nesting order.
- **Stack approach** – push each opener; on each closer, pop the top and verify it matches the closer's type using a map.
- **Two failure paths** – empty stack when a closer arrives (unmatched close), non-empty stack at the end (unmatched opens).
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(n) space; each character is pushed and popped at most once.
- **Java practice** – use `ArrayDeque` through `Deque` rather than the legacy `Stack` class.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking approval slips on a spike. Every time a nested approval opens, she spikes a slip of that color on top. When an approval closes, she can only remove the slip currently on top, and its color must match the one closing. If a red approval tries to close while a blue slip sits on top, the paperwork is out of order and the batch is rejected. At the end the spike must be empty.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Validation of "({[]})"
  ──────────────────────

  Char  Action              Stack
  ────  ──────────────────  ──────────
  (     push                [ ( ]
  {     push                [ {  ( ]
  [     push                [ [  {  ( ]
  ]     pop [ match ] ✓     [ {  ( ]
  }     pop { match } ✓     [ ( ]
  )     pop ( match ) ✓     [ ] empty

  Stack empty → VALID
```

```text
  Failure on "({)}"
  ─────────────────
  (     push                [ ( ]
  {     push                [ {  ( ]
  )     pop { expect ( → MISMATCH ✗

  → INVALID
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Balanced parentheses validation uses a stack because brackets must close in the reverse order they opened, which is LIFO. I scan the string once, push each opener, and on each closer I pop and verify the types match using a small map. The two failure conditions are an empty stack when a closer arrives and a non-empty stack after the full scan, and both are essential for correctness.

The algorithm runs in O(n) time with O(n) worst-case space. I use `ArrayDeque` through the `Deque` interface rather than the legacy `Stack` class, and I keep the matching in a `Map<Character, Character>` from closer to expected opener, which makes the logic clean and easily extensible to new bracket types.

This technique is the gateway to real parsing. The identical stack discipline validates HTML/XML tags, nested expressions, and balanced quotes. In production, running a bracket check before the full parser rejects malformed input early, saving the parser from wasting resources on corrupt data.

In my project at the National Bank of India, I used this as a pre-check on structured transaction messages with nested bracket segments. Malformed messages are rejected to a dead-letter path before the real parser ever sees them, giving the operations team a clean audit trail of every rejected message.

Remember one sentence: push every opener, pop and type-match on every closer, and the string is valid only if the stack ends empty.
